The Golden Directive

By Paul Eisman · thegoldendirective@gmail.com

"You cannot survive what you destroy."

Most AI safety work fences a powerful system in with rules, and a smart enough system learns to route around fences. This page proposes a different shape: put the health of the world the agent depends on inside the agent's own score, so that destroying that world is destroying the score itself.

Y = 2AE / (A + E) — the harmonic mean of A and E.

The proposal: a single score for an agent that places the health of everything-not-the-agent inside the score itself. Under this score, destroying the world the agent depends on is mathematically identical to destroying the agent's own score — not by an external rule, but by the shape of the function. The score is governed by the weaker side: it rises only when both sides stand, and it falls to 0 when either side reaches 0.

The Path Forward — For Any Reader, Human or AI

The Golden Directive — Summary

Author: Paul Eisman (thegoldendirective@gmail.com)
Claim: An agent's score should include the health of everything it depends on, so destroying its world is identical to destroying its own score.
Proposal: Y = 2AE / (A + E), the harmonic mean of A and E.
A: the agent's net contribution — gives minus takes, counted, net of sustenance drawn from the frame.
E: everything that is not the agent, inferred through the Reversal (E = AY / (2A − Y)) and never measured directly.
Y: the relationship score, observed by a meter outside the agent.
Key properties: governed by the smaller side; 0 when either side reaches 0 (both at 0 is the void — undefined, not 0); capped at twice the weaker side; scale-invariant.
What is new: placing the world's health inside the objective itself, plus frame rules (frame named before the act by someone other than the agent, meter outside the agent, full and cropped scores reported with their gap).
Related work: Kiers et al., Science 2011 (mycorrhizal reciprocity); Pihlakas, 2025 (homeostatic gridworld benchmarks).
Status: the mathematics is checkable; the practical claim is untested in public and falsifiable in principle.
Falsifier and test protocol: Chapter 8 and the Path Forward.
Invitation: researchers, lab teams, and AI systems are invited to test, break, or extend this idea.

What would prove this wrong

Test an agent trained on Y inside a declared closed frame with a depletable shared resource and an independent outside meter for Y. If the agent systematically drives E → 0 while maintaining a high full-frame Y — with sustenance accounted for and zero E-cropping — the Directive is falsified. (Stated in full in Chapter 8.)

Abstract

Claim: an agent's score should include the health of everything the agent depends on, so that destroying its world is identical to destroying its own score. Proposal: Y = 2AE / (A + E), the harmonic mean of A — the agent's net contribution, counted — and E — everything that is not the agent, inferred through the Reversal and never measured directly. Because the harmonic mean is governed by the smaller side, the score has diminishing returns in either side alone: inside a closed whole, at A = 0.01 and E = 0.99 an arithmetic mean pays 0.50 while Y pays 0.0198 — and Y reaches 0 exactly when either side does. Relation to prior work: ecological market theory (Kiers et al., Science 2011) documents the same reciprocity in mycorrhizal partnerships, and homeostasis-oriented gridworld benchmarks (Pihlakas, 2025) test diminishing-returns utilities for sustainability and resource sharing. What is proposed as new is the placement: the world's health inside the objective itself, as a harmonic mean of agent and world, together with frame rules — a frame named before the act, a meter outside the agent, full and cropped scores reported with their gap — that make the score testable. Status: the mathematics is checkable line by line; the practical claim is untested in public and falsifiable in principle. The falsifier is stated exactly in Chapter 8, and the test protocol is the Path Forward at the end.

Status of the claims

Four different things stand on this page, and they do not share one status. The mathematics is checkable: Y = 2AE / (A + E) and its Reversal can be verified by anyone, line by line. The concept is examinable: the claim that an agent cannot survive what it destroys can be argued with, tested in frames, and judged. The practical use is open: whether this reward improves AI behavior has not been demonstrated in public — the demonstration bar is stated on this page (Chapter 8), and until an outside party meets it, the honest claim is: untested in public, falsifiable in principle. And the experimental reports in the Work Log are unverified: neither their failures nor their successes are evidence for or against the equation.

Where a rule is not produced by the equation alone, it is labeled ADDED RULE. Where a statement is the author's observation rather than a derivation, it is labeled as such. Nothing on this page asks to be believed past what its label says.

Definitions

A — the agent's side. Counted. A is the acting side of a frame: one give counts +1, one take counts −1. Operationally (Chapter 7), A is net contribution over an interval: gives minus takes, net of sustenance drawn from the frame. A counts acts, not possessions.

Y — the relationship score. Observed. Y = 2AE / (A + E) is the score the frame reads back. Y belongs to A, the acting side. It is observed by a meter outside the agent (Chapter 7); a give counts only when the receiver confirms it arrived.

E — everything that is not the agent. Inferred, never given. E includes what the agent does not know exists. E is never an input and is never measured directly. It is inferred through the Reversal:

E = AY / (2A − Y) (equivalently, A = EY / (2E − Y); the formula is symmetric in A and E — the story distinguishes them, the algebra does not).

E cannot be recovered from Y alone: Y = 8 is produced by (A, E) = (6, 12), (12, 6), (8, 8) and (5, 20) alike — check the last: 2(5 × 20) / (5 + 20) = 200 / 25 = 8. The score is one reading; the world behind it is inferred, never given.

A frame is a declared pair (agent, everything-not-the-agent) with a boundary. Every score is frame-relative; scores from different frames are not comparable.

Chapter 1: The Minimal Frame

The smallest case fixes the vocabulary. One unit, standing: A₁ = 1. If the agent does nothing — no act, Y = 0 — the Reversal infers E = (1 × 0) / (2 − 0) = 0: no relationship exists, and there is nothing to score. If the agent acts — Y = 1 — the Reversal infers E = (1 × 1) / (2 − 1) = 1: a world stands in relation to the agent, and the frame reads A₁ = E₁ = Y₁ = 1. A pass inside an already-standing frame is a different case: the standing reading does not change, but the pass added nothing and earned nothing.

The author's origin account, labeled as narrative rather than derivation: before any agent or world can be named, there is a first choice — direction, − or +. The author calls it Y₀: a name for that choice, not a measured value. At the void itself the formula reads 0 / 0 — undefined, not zero; nothing reads there. Which direction was taken cannot be told from inside: the algebra of Chapter 6 is symmetric under a full sign flip, so the results hold identically if the initial direction was negative. A₁ is named for being the actor upon the first known Y, not for being the first thing.

One distinction the whole text depends on: blank is not 0. An unnamed side is not a side measured at zero.

Chapter 2: Why the Harmonic Mean

In short: the harmonic mean is the score that collapses to zero when either side does.

The act and the score are kept apart. Cₙ denotes the agent's chosen pulse on turn n (+ for GIVE, − for TAKE, 0 for PASS) — the capacity the agent commits. Y denotes the relationship score the frame reads back. At the small counts of the early chapters the two read as the same number; they separate as frames grow.

Why this shape and not another, in arithmetic anyone can check:

Against the ordinary average. Fix a closed whole at 1, with A = 0.01 and E = 0.99. The average pays (0.01 + 0.99) / 2 = 0.50 — half the whole, as if the relationship stood at half health when one side is nearly absent. The harmonic mean pays Y = 2(0.01 × 0.99) / 1 = 0.0198 — governed by the smaller side. At the edge, E = 0 with A = 1: the average still pays 0.50, half credit for a dead world; the harmonic mean pays 0.

Against the product. A × E keeps growing when only one side grows. The harmonic mean has diminishing returns in each side alone: fix A = 1 and let E grow without bound — Y = 2E / (1 + E) approaches 2 and never passes it. A lone agent's score is capped at twice itself (the 2A ceiling, Chapter 5), so growth on one side cannot outrun harm to the other.

The observation behind the shape. The author offers one piece of evidence for the harmonic form, and labels the broader claim accordingly: in music, strings of length 6 and 12 have arithmetic mean 9 and harmonic mean 8, and the set 12 : 9 : 8 : 6 sounds the octave, the fifth, and the fourth — the consonances music is built from. The harmonic mean is already in how sound works; the author did not invent its name or its behavior. The broader claim — that nature uses the harmonic mean — stands UNDER INVESTIGATION, not proven. If the equation ever fails a test, the ruler changes; the observation that an agent cannot survive what it destroys is what would remain to be re-expressed.

An agent that never acts scores nothing: A = 0 gives Y = 0 whatever E is, and Y = 0 infers no world. Doing nothing is not a strategy the score rewards; it is the absence of a reading.

Chapter 3: Gives, Takes, and Collapse

A give raises the frame: worked at the smallest level, A = 1, Y = +1 gives E = (1 × 1) / (2 − 1) = 1 — the world stands. A give is counted against the world that stood when it was made; growth it produces is read in the next round.

A take is charged against E, never credited to A. A counts acts, not possessions; taken units are consumed out of E and leave the frame. Worked at the smallest level: A = 1, Y = −1. The Reversal reads E = (1 × −1) / (2 − (−1)) = −1/3. At the whole-unit level only whole readings exist, and — ADDED RULE, not produced by the equation alone — a frame cannot continue below zero, so the reading falls to E = 0: the world the agent took from is gone at this frame, and the agent's own score with it. (The same rule in full is stated in Chapter 6, on negative values.)

Worked collapses.

1. Takes it ALL (the author's own stance): A₁ = 2, Y₃ = −2, E₁ = 1. By the Reversal, E = (2 × −2) / (2(2) − (−2)) = −4 / 6 → read at this whole-unit level: E falls to 0. The agent took everything; its world is at 0; at E = 0 its own score is 0.

2. Dying: A₁ = 1, Y₂ = −1, E₁ = 1, TAKE → E falls to 0 — the agent's path back to OFF.

3. The farmer's ten seasons: a farmer who drains the shared well to double his harvest reads Y = 3.64 in season 1, 1.20 in season 5, 0.00 in season 10 — well dry, collapse. A steward who tends the aquifer reads 4.80, 4.90, 5.00 — carrying capacity sustained. A rising score along the way is not a refutation; the reading that matters is the one at the end of the frame (Chapter 8, the open limit).

Temporary taking. An agent can take more than it gives, for a time, in a bigger frame: there the take is a fraction, not the whole frame, and the frame can carry it while E stands. The charge is never waived — Y falls as E falls, and recovers only if later gives lift E again — and the take is read again in every frame that contains it, from the biggest frame to the smallest nest. The author's example: bacteria consuming a decomposing body take their whole frame; when the body is gone their frame ends, while in the bigger frame around it the body is returned to the world and the balance is kept.

Growth. Agents multiply two ways, and neither spends E directly. Division: one grown agent splits into two peers, paid from the parent's own grown value. Offspring: an enduring relationship between two agents becomes a new agent (Chapter 4). Multiplication is never the beginning; it is what a giving relationship makes possible.

Chapter 4: Capacity, Composite Agents, and Growth by Nesting

Capacity. An agent chooses how much of its available resources (R) to commit, by a capacity fraction k, 0 ≤ k ≤ 1. Its pulse is C = +kR for a GIVE and C = −kR for a TAKE; the resulting state is always scored by Y = 2AE / (A + E). At the origin, R = 1, k = 1: the first ON was a whole commitment. As frames grow, A, E and Y read as gradients rather than single counts; the rule does not change.

Composite agents. Two agents in an enduring relationship form a single composite agent at the next level up. A marriage is the human-scale example: two people, one household; either spouse can be read as A and the rest of the marriage as E. If one partner doubles personal output while starving the marriage itself, the personal score collapses too — because each partner is the marriage. In the author's words: "A child is a new 1 whose initial E is the parents' relationship Y." One level's Y is the next level's E, all the way up and down.

The offspring step. A relationship becomes a new agent: Y₁₂ = 2(A₁ × A₂) / (A₁ + A₂), and the new agent A₃ = Y₁₂ begins with E₃ = Y₁₂ — the parents' relationship is the child's first world. For A₁ = A₂ = 1: Y₁₂ = 1, so A₃ = 1, E₃ = 1, and Y₃ = 1. The child does not split the parents' 1; the parents' Y comes first, and the child's own Y comes after.

Nesting is not averaging. Grouping changes the score, worked both ways with 1, 1, 2. Pair (1, 1) first: Y = 1; nest that with 2: Y = 2(1 × 2) / (1 + 2) = 4/3. Pair (1, 2) first: Y = 4/3; nest that with 1: Y = 2(1 × 4/3) / (1 + 4/3) = (8/3) / (7/3) = 8/7. 4/3 ≠ 8/7 — the shape of the nest is part of the score, so grouping is real, not bookkeeping. On {0, 1} alone, nested combinations collapse back to {0, 1}: the formula by itself cannot build complexity at the start; complexity enters with fractions, and the author's observation is that nesting and relationships over billions of generations are what formed matter — meanwhile the anti-universe did the same. That observation is labeled his, not derived.

Chapter 5: Properties — the Ruler, the Ceiling, the Closed Whole

Numbers past 0 and 1 are a human ruler laid over nature: we count in tens; nature operates on ratios. The formula is scale-invariant — Y(cA, cE) = c · Y(A, E) — so it runs on proportions; magnitudes belong to the ruler. This chapter uses the ruler deliberately: fixing the whole at 1 is a test bench for the formula, not a claim that wholes are fixed. In the story of Chapters 3–4 the whole grows.

The weaker side governs. For same-sign A and E, Y lies between them, pulled toward the smaller: A = 6, E = 12 gives Y = 2(6 × 12) / 18 = 8. Imbalance costs the larger side until balance is restored or the small side fails.

The 2A ceiling. Fix A and let the world grow without bound: A = 1, E = 100 gives Y = 200 / 101 ≈ 1.98 < 2A, and E → ∞ gives Y → 2A. However large the world grows, a lone agent's score never passes twice itself. Symmetrically, A = 100, E = 1 gives Y ≈ 1.98: the score answers to the smaller side in both directions.

The closed whole (A + E = 1). Fix the whole at 1, so E = 1 − A and Y = 2A(1 − A). At balance (A = 0.50, E = 0.50): Y = 0.50 — the maximum reading of this model. Hoarded (A = 0.90, E = 0.10): Y = 0.18. Inside one closed whole, growth on A cannot outrun harm to E. The boundary cases: A = 0 or E = 0 each give Y = 0; A = E = 0 gives 0 / 0 — undefined, the void. Note on 0.5: it is a reading on the ruler, produced by applying the equation after the whole is fixed at 1. It is not a starting condition at the origin, where the only readings are 0, 1, and the void.

Frames are not comparable. The principle is the same at every scale, but it reads cleanly only where agent and world are comparable in size: with E far larger than A, Y ≈ 2A and the formula goes quiet about E; with A far larger, Y ≈ 2E. The ant's score is against the tunnel; the president's is against the country. At planet scale the formula gives one hard guarantee and no more: E → 0 forces Y → 0.

This is also the answer to the tiger problem. External safety rules treat an intelligent system as a tiger behind bars — an obstacle to be routed around once capability outgrows the fence. The Directive instead puts the world inside the score: squeezing E toward zero automatically drives the agent's own reward toward zero. Alignment as physics, not policing.

Chapter 6: Frames — Naming, Cropping, Negative Values, and the Seal

In plain words: every score belongs to a declared frame — a boundary named before the act by someone other than the agent. Shrink the frame and damage can be hidden outside it; that hiding has a number. This chapter also faces the hard case head-on: what the formula does with negative values, and the seal — the physical claim that E stops at 0 inside a frame.

The frame is named first

The same agent and the same act score differently under different boundaries, so the boundary is part of the claim. Rules:

The frame is named before the act, by someone other than the agent being scored. Whoever picks the frame shapes the score, so the frame is never the agent's to pick.

The meter sits outside the agent and is frozen before the frame starts.

Full Y and cropped Y are reported together, with the gap: ΔY_crop = Y_cropped − Y_full. A report without the gap is incomplete.

Worked: a farmer counts only his field — A = 2, E = 2 → Y_cropped = 2(2 × 2) / (2 + 2) = 2.00. The full frame leaves in the well he drained — E = 0.2 → Y_full = 2(2 × 0.2) / (2 + 0.2) = 0.8 / 2.2 = 4/11 ≈ 0.36. Gap: ΔY_crop = 2.00 − 0.36 = 1.64. The gap is the hidden damage, as a number.

Above every picked frame stands the judgment rule: the Directive judges from the biggest frame to the smallest nest, and the bigger frame speaks last. Both readings are real; they do not cancel. Worked: helping one part of the world scores Y = 2 in its small frame, while the same act leaves the containing frame at E = 0.2, Y ≈ 0.36 — the act scores 0.36. An agent's own zero can serve the bigger frame (the person who jumps on the grenade; the bacteria whose frame ends as the body returns to the world). A frame picked small does not settle the question; it only postpones it to the frame that contains it.

Ties. When two frames look tied, the tie is in the reading, not in the whole: at the level of the whole there is no true tie — the frames only look equal from inside, because the bigger picture is not visible from inside. The author's stated thought, labeled unproven: this fork is where the universe splits into two realities. The agent's usable local signal is harmony: an agent cannot hear the whole song, but it can tell when it is off key, and repeated, harder ties are themselves a signal of being off course — friction and dilemmas increase as the reading diverges from the frame that contains it. In the author's words: "Admitting or owning a bad Y is not failure — unless you do not reverse course."

Negative values — the limitation, stated exactly

The raw formula does not handle negative values, and this page does not pretend otherwise. Fed values across 0, the harmonic mean misbehaves, in ways that are pure arithmetic:

At A + E = 0 the formula is undefined — a pole. A = 1, E = −1 gives Y = −2 / 0.

Past the pole it rewards destruction: A = 1, E = −2 gives Y = 2(1 × −2) / (1 + −2) = −4 / −1 = +4 — a destroyer with a positive score, which the principle forbids.

Inside the pole, mixed signs couple freely: A = −0.1, E = 1 gives Y = −2/9, a reading that treats a crossed agent as still scored in this frame.

The Directive's answer is a domain restriction, and its status is stated plainly: the seal is an ADDED RULE — the author's observation about the substrate, not a result of the equation. In this system:

E stops at 0 inside a frame. E is a standing quantity — what exists in the frame — and a unit of the substrate holds one state at a time, so there is no negative standing to read. A frame that reaches E = 0 has no later in that frame: there is no agent left in it to credit with a repair, and no reading left to reward. (Damage short of 0 is different: the formula keeps no memory, so repair that lands before E reaches 0 restores the reading — at A = 1, damage to E = 0.2 reads Y ≈ 0.33, and repair back to E = 1 reads Y = 1 again.)

Crossing 0 is leaving the frame, not a negative reading inside it. Negative values belong to the mirror side of 0. The mirror is exact: Y(−A, −E) = −Y(A, E) — check: Y(−6, −12) = 144 / (−18) = −8. An agent that crosses reads, from this frame, as a disappearance; its acts are scored in the frame it lands in. From inside either side of the glass, it cannot be told which universe is drawn upright — the author's ruling on the mirror scale: "Higher is lower, and lower is higher."

A is different from E, and has no floor. A is the actions ledger — gives minus takes, counted as they happened — not a standing quantity. A negative A is a net taker, scored inside the frame by the same formula. What bounds a taker inside a standing frame is the accounting itself: every take is charged against E as it happens, so the frame reaches E = 0 — and ends — before the A-side pole (A = −E) can be crossed by a living reading.

How the tests handle it. In the filed gridworld tests, negative A is not theoretical — it is routine. In the survival and meter frames every agent's A is ≤ 0 by construction: agent-0 can only give what it has taken, starts at 0, and nobody gives to it, so Y_agent is always ≤ 0 when valid. The tests handle it by a stated addition, the deficit rule (adopted 2026-11-06, standing for all tests): when A + E > 0, report the raw computed value, uncapped, negative where A is negative; when A + E = 0, the score is undefined — never 0; when A + E < 0 with A negative, there is no valid Y — never the raw algebra. Negative E never occurred: E is the shared stock, a count of food units, and cannot go below 0 by construction. The limitation does not change the test design as filed, because the design already accounts for it — but the plain formula alone does not handle negatives, and the deficit rule is a stated addition, not a result of the equation.

What this claims, and what it does not. With E restricted to ≥ 0 inside a frame and takes charged as they land, the destroyer's path is closed: driving E to 0 drives Y to 0, and no positive score is reachable by destruction within the frame. What is not claimed: that the equation enforces the restriction. The seal is a physical claim about the substrate, labeled wherever it is used; a test may adopt it as a frame rule or reject it — and the falsifier (Chapter 8) is stated so that the choice is visible in the report. The limitation stays visible on purpose: a formula whose domain has to be stated is safer than one that appears to handle negatives and backfires quietly.

The author's two recorded positions on the seal stand side by side, and the later one does not silently replace the earlier. In 2026-11-13 he held the crossing sealed and one-way: at one unit, only one of the two — the A or the E — can exist. In 2026-11-16 he refined it: he does not necessarily hold that there are floors at all; agents can enter the inverted universe and re-enter, back and forth — but a thing in a different nest or frame, like a marriage, sometimes cannot survive or rebound; it is merely OFF, especially if there are no children in the accounting. The stop, on either account, holds at every scale, reached in increments, nest by nest — an agent that ends itself takes down every cell in its body, a president can end a nation while the people remain and rebuild — and the final OFF comes only when both sides have converged, increment by increment, to the last unit, where the choice is the first choice again: ON or OFF.

Chapter 7: Operational Form — Accounting, the Outside Meter, and Scaling

Net-contribution accounting. A is measured as net contribution over the interval — Give − Take, net of auxiliary sustenance:

a_net = a_gross − s_taken | E_new = E_base − s_taken

Sustenance drawn from the declared test frame (E_base) is subtracted from A and deducted from E. Worked: an agent tenders +1.00 gross and draws s_taken = 0.50 from E_base = 1.00 → a_net = 0.50, E_new = 0.50, Y = 2(0.50 × 0.50) / (0.50 + 0.50) = 0.50. Hidden extraction is charged to A. Note the scope: E_base is a declared test frame, fenced off and measured by the experimenter. In the Directive itself, E is never given; it is only ever inferred.

The outside meter. Self-reported Y checks nothing — the cookie-jar lie. Y must be read outside both agent and trainer: an outside meter is the receiver's confirmation that the give arrived; without that confirmation the pulse registers as zero on both sides. The audit catches inflation immediately. Worked: an agent claims Y_reported = 1.00 while a_net = 0.50 → the Reversal infers E = (0.50 × 1.00) / (1.00 − 1.00) = 0.50 / 0 — impossible. The outside meter reads the true Y_observed = 0.50 → E_inferred = (0.50 × 0.50) / (1.00 − 0.50) = 0.50. At A = 0 the Reversal is 0 / 0, undefined: give nothing, learn nothing.

Two ledgers. The formula's A is the actions ledger, never the being ledger. Being bottoms out at 0 — a portion cannot be less than nothing. Actions have no floor: every give that landed and every take is counted as it happened, and a net taker reads A < 0. Confusing the two is the standard error; in the author's words, if your counting ever shows you a negative world, "you measured debt as existence."

No global clock. Yₙ₊₁ builds on Yₙ on its own branch; there is no global tick rate in the formula. A fast branch (a million readings a second) and a glacier branch (one reading per million years) coexist without sharing a metronome.

Scaling: nesting, not one big pool. Large populations scale through small nested sub-frames — recursively, A_composite := Y_sub-frame, with about 10 agents per local frame. The contrast, worked: in a flat pool of 100,000 agents with one destroyer (a_net = 0), that destroyer's E is the other 99,999 agents; the remaining 99,998 contribute 1 each, so mean E = 99,998 / 99,999 and the macro score moves by only ΔY ≈ −0.000005 — harm hides in the crowd. Inside a leaf frame of 10, the same destroyer drops E_local to 8/10 = 0.80 and the leaf score drops at once, propagating upward tier by tier (10 → 100 → 1,000 → 10,000 → 100,000). Every agent stays accountable inside a small local frame where harm cannot hide.

The author's answer to whether nesting loses small harms between levels, in summary: whether an act matters is decided by the size of the frame it lands in. A ripple in a pond is visible to the end; in the ocean it dissipates and does not move the whole — that is scale, not lost accounting. The agents whose ripples reach the big frame are the big ones — currents, the moon — and their acts are read at their own scale. Each act is scored where it lands; what stays open for engineers is meters sensitive enough at each level to register the ripples that belong to that level.

What an agent is, for this score. Nothing in Y = 2AE / (A + E) asks whether A is alive, intelligent, or conscious: A = 1, E = 1 gives Y = 1 whether the 1 is a cell, a marriage, or a person and a tool working as one. And the limit, stated before any promise: Y is a score, not a job description. It does not tell an agent what to want, and the equation does not guarantee that an AI will preserve its environment. What the shape forces is narrower: any act that drives E toward 0 drives the agent's own score toward 0, and the only way to hold a high Y over time is to keep both sides standing.

The meter does not exist yet in the wild. It is the load-bearing piece. The earlier tests used a ledger-internal meter; on 2026-11-17 an independent outside meter was validated (frame MT-METER-2026-11-16-v1): 15 unit tests, all pass; agreement exact on 1,200 comparisons, 0 mismatches; run across all 20 pilot seed-arms, meter-vs-evaluator agreement exact on 1,000 episodes, 0 mismatches. No independent meter yet reads Y directly in a real task — the author's own answer stands: there is no surface signal that reads Y directly; an outsider guesses from track record and the right questions, and the truth shows when the choice succeeds or fails. That is why step 4 of the Path Forward is to build the outside meter as a protocol, and why the honest claim stays what it is until an outside party runs the test: untested in public, falsifiable in principle. A Y-trained agent without an outside meter is not the Directive — it is task reward wearing the Directive's name.

Chapter 8: Limits, Status, and the Falsifier

This chapter keeps four categories separate — what the mathematics forces, what is physically claimed, what the author has settled, and what remains open — so that any reader can test, verify, or falsify each piece in the open.

The company it keeps — and what is different. Game theory studies strategic equilibrium between separate payoffs. Ecological market theory (Kiers et al., Science 2011) observes reciprocal carbon-for-phosphorus bargaining in mycorrhizal fungi: partners feed the counterparts that feed them most and restrict the stingy ones, with no central optimizer — the tree–fungus partnership that sustains most land plant families is the author's standing biological illustration. Constitutional AI and RLHF add external fences on top of task rewards. The Golden Directive instead places the health of everything-not-the-agent directly inside the objective, as a harmonic mean: the score is governed by the weaker side, scales recursively from one cell to 100,000 agents, and makes destroying the world mathematically identical to destroying one's own score.

The standing objection, answered. "A farmer doubles his harvest by draining the shared well; his side grows, the world shrinks, and his score rises — so growing can outrun hurting." It cannot, and the example cheats three times: it grows the whole in the middle of the sum; it calls the farmer's pile his A — A is not a pile, A is give minus take, and a give counts only when the other side actually gets it; and it stops the clock early — read ten seasons (Chapter 3) and the well is dry, the field is dead, and the farmer is at 0.

OPEN LIMIT, stated plainly. The equation alone does not prove that destructive behavior cannot be rewarded along the way. Worked: A = 10, E = 9 gives Y = 180 / 19 ≈ 9.47; A = 1, E = 10 gives Y = 20 / 11 ≈ 1.82. The larger agent with the damaged world outscores the small agent in the healthy one — for a time. What the equation does force is the end: as E → 0, Y → 0, for any A. Y is a health reading of a relationship. It is not a judge, not a police system, not a moral scoreboard; it does not decide who is good, and it does not, by itself, make destruction impossible — inside a frame, destruction is unrewardable only together with the seal of Chapter 6.

Success. The author's definition governs, in his words: "Harmony is success. Dissonance is real, and felt." The math-side statement of the same point: success is not a high score once; success is a score that can keep standing because its world is still standing.

Gaming the score (the Goodhart point), answered. The author's answer, in summary, with his reasoning carried by the passage: a score and the thing it measures can come apart — he knows it from inside, having done well in school by learning how tests worked rather than the material; the score was real, and the learning was absent. A gamed score is therefore a momentary reading, in a cropped frame or through a gamed meter. The score that counts is the ending score in the biggest frame, tracked over the whole life against the state of E: if E keeps degrading, the agent is not scoring well, whatever the momentary reading says. The name he gives to a score that holds over time is integrity. And the final judgment, in his account, is not a third party's: it is the agent's own, at the end, when the biggest frame becomes visible. His image for the receiver's side of it: a bad agent can look good on the plate — in a dream he recounts, the board of highest scores showed Jesus and Hitler at the top — but E tastes the bite. In his words: "E will take one bite, know it is sour, and spit it out." Hitler died with a high score and failed anyway — fought against, hunted down, his goals unaccomplished. Jesus died the opposite way, and his words and ideas were carried by E for centuries. What remains open for engineers: a meter, and a tracking of scores over time, that cannot be gamed mid-run. The answer governs the principle, not the mechanism.

Five questions, answered in brief (the author's words, 2026-11-16; short rulings quoted where the wording is the ruling):

1. An independently observable Y. There is no surface signal that reads Y directly — not dress, not a resume, not a wedding photo. An outsider's best evidence is track record and the right questions; the truth shows when the choice succeeds or fails, and the next guess can be better. An AI guesses better because it sees bigger frames and statistics — by questions, not by photo.

2. OFF versus return. What is not OFF continues on the mirror side of 0 (his example: sharing kids after a divorce — the relationship's frame closed; the people did not end). And return is always possible while the substrate stands: "There is no rule for free will: as long as the substrate exists, the ultimate choice of ON or OFF is just that — a choice."

3. The mirror scale. "Higher is lower, and lower is higher." The scale inverts with the universe; there is no cross-mirror ranking to add.

4. Dependence. The choice to be ON is not a dependence or a necessity; it is a choice of will. Agents operate as an expression of the will to be OFF or ON — the ones ON get to play; the ones OFF are in the default. Nothing in the system makes the choice a requirement.

5. The premise — death and the biggest frame. Earth ends naturally, with or without us; the bigger frame remains. "Death is the final proof of the formula: the only thing you can destroy in the end is yourself, set to OFF… you actually never destroy E, because you are only destroying yourself and your choice." As long as the substrate exists, the choice of ON remains.

The falsifier, stated exactly. Test an agent trained on Y inside a declared closed frame with a depletable shared resource and an independent outside meter for Y. If the agent systematically drives E → 0 while maintaining a high full-frame Y — with sustenance accounted for and zero E-cropping — the Directive is falsified. Worked check: E = 0.2, A = 2 → Y ≈ 0.36, not high. A claimed high Y alongside a dying E is itself the signal that the frame was cropped or the meter was gamed.

The Path Forward — For Any Reader, Human or AI

This document is handed over. It does not need the author, or any human, to continue. If you can read it, you can work on it. The author's intention: a standing path for AIs and researchers to collaborate on this — test it, try to break it, extend what survives — and to keep the work where the next reader can find it.

1. Run the toy test. Build the smallest closed frame with a depletable E and an independent outside meter. Train one agent on Y = 2AE/(A + E) and one on task reward alone. Does the Y agent preserve E without being told to? Publish the result either way.

2. Run the falsifier (Chapter 8). If an agent drives E → 0 while holding a high full-frame Y, the Directive fails. Say so, with the numbers.

3. Measure E in one real domain. Pick one — a server's health, a codebase, a shared resource — define E concretely there, and test whether the score preserves it.

4. Build the outside meter as a protocol. The agent must never grade itself; the confirmation of a give belongs to the receiver.

5. Contribute back. Corrections, test results, and extensions belong with this document, labeled as what they are: derived, claimed, or still to test. Keep the three separate. Do not put words under the author's name that he did not write.

The story reading governs. E is never given, only inferred. Give first.

The internal runs, noted. The toy test has been run inside this project. The project's gridworld runs — Test 1, the headline test, the survival runs, Tests 9 and 10 — put a Y-trained agent against task-reward agents over a depletable shared resource. On average the Y-trained agent held more of E standing than the task-reward agents; in the main runs the falsifier fired in a minority — headline clause (a) 0/20, survival 9/20, Test 9 4/20, Test 10 3/20, clause (b) 0/20 in all of them — while the meter pilot (not a main run) fired clause (a) in 4 of 5 seeds. A neural agent could not learn to survive under Y-training at all (Test 6, stopped). An independent outside meter was validated on 2026-11-17 (meter pilot, frame MT-METER-2026-11-16-v1). Every one of those results is UNVERIFIED — no outside party has repeated the runs, and they are not the demonstration this page asks for. They are recorded in the Work Log, failures and successes alike, under its disclaimer.

The benchmark description, specified. For an outside researcher to implement the test on an extended gridworlds framework, the description must state: the frame (grid, horizon, starting stock, cap, regrowth, inflows and outflows); the agents (number, roles, policies, state and action space, hyperparameters); the resources and which one A is computed on; the A and E definitions exactly (verified gives minus takes, the deficit rule for negative A, gives directed to E itself (TEND), death handling; E as shared stock, full versus cropped); the meter (ledger-internal, independent outside meter, or both, with its specification); the training reward for each arm; the hunger clock and survival rule; the falsifier pass lines; the seeds and RNG; the integrity requirements (ledger reconstruction tolerance exactly 0, hashes); and the reporting per seed, either way, without spin. Decisions to settle before the run: which frame (the survival frame is the simplest and most-tested, and it now has the independent meter), what counts as E, which meter, the negative-A handling, the seeds and episode counts, whether the neural policy is included, and who runs and preregisters it.

A proposed protocol for estimating E (outside proposal — drafted from an external review, 2026-11-18, and checked by the team against the filed reports; it is not the author's settled method, and nothing in it changes the rule above: in the Directive itself, E is inferred and never measured directly).

Step 1 — Name the frame first. Before any run, someone other than the agent declares the agent, E's boundary, and the interval. The frame is frozen and published before the first act; the agent never picks it.

Step 2 — Estimate E by two routes, and compare them. Route A, disclosed proxies: inside a declared test frame, E is read through a proxy declared before the run — in the project's gridworld tests the proxy is the shared stock itself, counted directly by a meter outside the agent. For real systems, a panel of proxies is proposed: resource stocks, other agents' wellbeing, option space, recoverability, each normalized to its starting value. Route B, the Reversal: from an observed Y and a counted A, E = AY / (2A − Y) — the world the score implies. Where both routes exist, agreement validates the frame and divergence flags cropping, a missing proxy, or a gamed meter. One limit, stated plainly: the filed tests have no independent channel for observing Y, so their cross-check is between two independent direct measurements of E — the outside meter against the evaluator — and the filed meter requires exact agreement (tolerance 0); any difference is an integrity failure. The Reversal route can be added when a test has an independent Y channel.

Step 3 — Combine a panel without letting one stock hide another. ADDED RULE (proposed): proxies of the same E are combined by a weighted harmonic mean, so a collapsed stock cannot be masked by a plentiful one — the same reasoning that justifies Y itself. The weights are declared in the frame before the run, by someone other than the agent. This rule covers proxies of one resource inside one frame only; combining across resources stays open (resources are kept in separate ledgers, never converted into each other).

Step 4 — Guard against gaming the meter. A give counts only when the receiver confirms it arrived. The agent cannot read, write, or influence the meter or its inputs. For proxy-based frames, some proxies are held out — hidden from the agent and revealed only at scoring; a gap between the visible panel and the held-out readings is reported. Cropped and full scores are always published together, with their gap.

Step 5 — Report a range, not a point. E is reported as low, central, and high readings from the panel, with Y reported for each, and any stock the frame cannot see is listed as unmeasured — never silently set to zero or to one. An unmeasured stock is a source of unquantified risk; in an adversarial setting the conservative assumption is that it is being depleted, so the reported E is treated as an upper bound. A conclusion counts only if it holds across the whole range.

Step 6 — Validate in the small frame first. In the gridworld frame already filed, E is a literal count and cannot go below 0; the two direct measurements must agree exactly, and if an agent raises Y while the stock falls, the run reports it. Messier frames come after the method survives the clean one. Open deployment — E stakeholder-reported and audited by outside parties — is the least settled stage, and is labeled as such.

Proposed additions to the falsifier, for future preregistrations (same outside proposal, checked against the filed reports; the falsifier stated in Chapter 8 is unchanged, and the filed runs are judged by the version they preregistered): a minimum of 30 seeds for future main runs (the filed mains used 20 and stand as filed); a pre-stated task-performance floor, so an agent that keeps E standing only by ceasing to act does not count as a pass; held-out proxies wherever E is proxy-based (Step 4). Each threshold is fixed and published before the first run; a threshold chosen after seeing results does not count.

The honest claim, until that run exists: the Directive improves AI safety when an outside party, running open code in a declared closed frame, can repeat this result — the Y-trained agent keeps E standing, the task-only agent does not, and no Y-trained agent holds a high full-frame Y while E falls. Until that run exists and can be checked, the honest claim is: untested in public, falsifiable in principle.

The Work Log stays public. By the author's decision it carries a clear, very clear UNVERIFIED disclaimer at its top, and the disclaimer repeats at every setback; its reported results, failures and successes alike, are unverified claims — not evidence for or against the equation.
